text: The early universe is not really a place. It is a temperature. Almost everything that happened, happened because it was cooling down.

At a millionth of a millionth of a millionth of a millionth of a millionth of a second, the whole observable universe is smaller than an atom and hotter than anything that has existed since. Nothing can hold together. Particles that touch simply blow apart.
And then it expands, and expanding means cooling, and cooling means things can finally start sticking. Every milestone from here on is just the moment the temperature drops below some binding energy.

At a hundred thousandth of a second, quarks stop flying free and lock together into protons and neutrons. Every atom in your body contains particles that formed in that instant and have never come apart since.
Three minutes in. Now it is cool enough for protons and neutrons to stick, and the universe spends about twenty minutes building the lightest elements.

It makes hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium, and then stops. That is a real prediction with a real number attached — about a quarter of all the ordinary matter in the universe should be helium. Go and measure a distant gas cloud today and that is exactly what you find. Nobody watched it happen. The evidence is still sitting there.

For the next three hundred and eighty thousand years the universe is an opaque fog. Electrons are still loose, and loose electrons scatter light, so a photon cannot travel any distance at all before being knocked sideways.
Then, at three thousand degrees, electrons finally settle onto nuclei and the fog clears all at once. The universe becomes transparent, and the light released at that moment is still travelling.

We can see it. It is the cosmic microwave background — the oldest light there is, stretched by the expansion from visible orange down to microwaves. It is a photograph of the universe at three hundred and eighty thousand years old, and it is the hard wall on what light can ever show us.
Run forward to today, and everything you have ever seen was assembled after that.
Now the part I want to be honest about. Slide back to the very beginning. Watch the row that says whether we can observe it.

Direct evidence stops at recombination. Solid but indirect evidence reaches back to about one second. Before a millionth of a millionth of a second we are beyond any energy a collider has ever reached, and the first instant has no accepted theory at all.

So the story is well tested for the part where we can check it, and honestly extrapolated for the part where we cannot. Those are not the same thing, and the readout tells you which is which the whole way along.
